title: ACT English — Practice Test 1
summary: A full, timed enhanced-ACT English practice test: six original essays, 50 questions in 35 minutes, with an explanation for every answer.

blocks.text: This is a complete practice test for the **English section of the enhanced ACT**. The real English section has **50 questions in 35 minutes**, and **40 of those questions are scored**. The other questions are unscored field-test items, and you cannot tell which ones they are, so on test day you must treat every question as if it counts. In this practice test **all 50 questions count** towards your result.

The test has **six essays**. Five follow the design of the scored part of the real test: three essays of about 340 words with 10 questions each and two of about 185 words with 5 questions each. A sixth essay of about 340 words with 10 more questions brings the total to 50, just as on test day. The essays are informational, argumentative and narrative. Most questions ask about an **underlined portion** of the essay, and many offer **NO CHANGE** (choice A) if the original is already the best version. Other questions ask whether to add or delete a sentence, where a sentence belongs, or whether the essay achieves a goal.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone and nothing to help you. Have 35 minutes free.
Press Start: the timer runs for 35 minutes and the section ends automatically when time is up. On the real test you cannot go back to English once its time is over.

Each essay is shown again with every question, and only that question's portion is underlined and numbered with the question number, for example [7]. For placement questions, the sentences or paragraphs are numbered [1], [2] and so on.
Aim for about 42 seconds per question. Check the clock after every essay.
There is no penalty for wrong answers on the ACT, so answer every question. Use Mark for review and come back if you have time.
Your result is a practice score (number correct and a percentage), not an official ACT scaled score.

blocks.title: ACT English — Practice Test 1
blocks.intro: Six essays (Passages I–VI), 50 questions, 35 minutes. For each question, read the essay and choose the best answer. For underlined portions, choose the version that is correct, clear and fits the essay best; choose NO CHANGE if the original is best. In the real test 40 of the 50 questions are scored and the rest are unscored field-test items; here all 50 count. Every question has an explanation in the review after you finish.

questions.p:
**Passage I**
**The Reed Pen**

Every morning except Friday, my grandfather unlocked the green shutters of his shop on a narrow lane near Al-Azhar Street. Inside, the air smelled of ink and old paper. He was a calligrapher, and for fifty years he __[1] had written__ shop signs, wedding invitations, and verses for the walls of homes across Cairo. When I was twelve, my parents sent me to spend the summer with him. I expected to be bored, instead I found a world that moved at the speed of a reed pen.

On my first day, he handed me a dried reed and a small knife. "Before you write a single letter," he said, "you must learn to cut your own pen." He showed me how to slice the tip at an angle and split it down the middle so that the ink would flow evenly. My first ten pens cracked. For example, my grandfather simply placed another reed on the table and waited.

By July, I was allowed to practice the letter alif, a single vertical stroke. It looks like the easiest letter in the alphabet, but it appears in a great many Arabic words. My grandfather checked each one against a column of tiny diamond-shaped dots, the old system calligraphers use to measure a letter's height. Mine were always too short or too thick.

One afternoon, a woman came in with a photograph of her late father's handwriting and asked whether he could copy a line from it onto a wall plaque. He worked on it for three days. When she returned, she looked at the plaque silently for a long time without saying a single word, and then she cried. After she left, my grandfather wiped his pen and said, "The hand is only the servant of the heart."

I am a university student now, and I write most things on a keyboard. Still, I keep a reed pen on my desk, it's tip cut at the angle my grandfather taught me. Whenever I feel rushed, I write a single alif, slowly, and measure it against a column of dots.
questions.q: Question 1 (underlined portion [1]): Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: NO CHANGE is right: the past perfect "had written" shows fifty years of work that happened before the past moment of the story ("He was a calligrapher"). "Has written" wrongly mixes the present perfect into a past narrative, "writes" shifts to the present, and "had wrote" uses the wrong verb form (the past participle is "written").

Question 3 (point [3] in the passage): At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
"Some calligraphers today prefer pens made of bamboo or even metal."
Should the writer make this addition here?
c: Yes, because it explains why the narrator's first ten pens cracked.
Yes, because it shows that the grandfather's methods were old-fashioned.
No, because it interrupts the account of the narrator's first lesson with a general detail about other kinds of pens.

questions.q: Question 10: Suppose the writer's goal had been to write a brief history of Arabic calligraphy. Would this essay accomplish that goal?
c: Yes, because it explains the system of dots that calligraphers use to measure letters.
Yes, because it describes how a reed pen is cut and prepared.

questions.p:
**Passage II**
**Farms in the Sky**

Look down from a tall building in almost any large city, and you will see a landscape of flat, empty roofs. To a growing number of urban farmers, __[11] those rooftops, are__ wasted land. Across the world, people are turning them into small farms that produce vegetables, herbs, and even eggs.

Growing food on a roof is not as simple as carrying soil upstairs. Wet soil is heavy, but most roofs cannot hold a deep layer of it. Many rooftop farmers therefore use lightweight growing materials such as, a mix of compost and crushed volcanic rock, or they grow plants in shallow trays. Others use hydroponics, a method in which plant roots sits in nutrient-rich water rather than in soil. Before any farm is built, an engineer must check that the building can safely carry the extra weight.

Rooftop farms offer benefits beyond the food they produce. A layer of plants shades the roof and helps keep the floors below cooler in summer, which can reduce the need for air conditioning. Plants also absorb some of the rainwater that would otherwise rush into city drains during a storm. In addition, the farms give people in crowded neighborhoods a chance to work with plants and to buy vegetables that were picked freshly from the plants that grew them only a few hours before.

Rooftop farming does have limits. Wind can be super intense on a high roof, and water must be carried or pumped up from below. Most rooftop farms are also too small to feed a whole city. Supporters reply that rooftop farms were never meant to replace those in the countryside; they are meant to add fresh food close to the people who eat it.

On one apartment block in Giza, for instance, a group of neighbors led by agricultural engineer Nadia Fawzy grows tomatoes, mint, and lettuce in rows of shallow trays. The harvest is modest, and nobody expects it to replace the local market. Still, the neighbors say that the roof, once used only for storing broken furniture, has become the friendliest place in the building.
questions.q: Question 11 (underlined portion [11]): Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: Never put a single comma between a subject ("those rooftops") and its verb ("are"); the key removes it. "Being" is not a main verb, and "which are" turns the rest into a clause that leaves the sentence without a main verb, so both create fragments.

**Farms in the Sky**

Look down from a tall building in almost any large city, and you will see a landscape of flat, empty roofs. To a growing number of urban farmers, those rooftops, are wasted land. Across the world, people are turning them into small farms that produce vegetables, herbs, and even eggs.

Growing food on a roof is not as simple as carrying soil upstairs. Wet soil is heavy, but most roofs cannot hold a deep layer of it. Many rooftop farmers therefore use lightweight growing __[13] materials such as, a mix__ of compost and crushed volcanic rock, or they grow plants in shallow trays. Others use hydroponics, a method in which plant roots sits in nutrient-rich water rather than in soil. Before any farm is built, an engineer must check that the building can safely carry the extra weight.

Rooftop farms offer benefits beyond the food they produce. A layer of plants shades the roof and helps keep the floors below cooler in summer, which can reduce the need for air conditioning. Plants also absorb some of the rainwater that would otherwise rush into city drains during a storm. In addition, the farms give people in crowded neighborhoods a chance to work with plants and to buy vegetables that were picked freshly from the plants that grew them only a few hours before.

Rooftop farming does have limits. Wind can be super intense on a high roof, and water must be carried or pumped up from below. Most rooftop farms are also too small to feed a whole city. Supporters reply that rooftop farms were never meant to replace those in the countryside; they are meant to add fresh food close to the people who eat it.

On one apartment block in Giza, for instance, a group of neighbors led by agricultural engineer Nadia Fawzy grows tomatoes, mint, and lettuce in rows of shallow trays. The harvest is modest, and nobody expects it to replace the local market. Still, the neighbors say that the roof, once used only for storing broken furniture, has become the friendliest place in the building.

questions.p:
**Passage III**
**The Long Road to the Modern Bicycle**

In 1817, a German __[21] inventor named Karl Drais__ introduced a wooden "running machine" with two wheels and no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet. In the 1860s, makers in France attached pedals directly to the front wheel. These machines were nicknamed "boneshakers" because their wooden wheels, covered with iron, made every bump painful.

Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, the only way to travel farther with each turn of the pedals was to make that wheel bigger. By the 1870s, the high-wheeler, with a front wheel that could reach a grown man's chest—had become popular with daring young riders. Riders sat high above that wheel, and a sudden stop could throw them headfirst over the handlebars.

The real breakthrough came in the 1880s with the "safety bicycle." It had two wheels of similar size and a chain that connected the pedals to the rear wheel. Because the rider sat lower, between the wheels, falls were far less dangerous. Air-filled rubber tires, introduced soon afterward, made the ride far smoother and less bumpy. The basic design has changed surprisingly little since then.
questions.q: Question 21 (underlined portion [21]): Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: NO CHANGE is right: "named Karl Drais" is essential information that tells us which inventor, so it takes no commas. A comma after "named" splits the verb from its object, a comma after "Drais" separates the subject from its verb "introduced," and a semicolon must join two complete sentences.

questions.p:
**Passage IV**
**Let Teenagers Sleep**

At many high schools, the first class begins before eight o'clock. For a lot of teenagers, that means __[26] waking up in the dark and to arrive__ at school still half asleep. Some schools have tried different timetables over the years. Many adults believe that teenagers could solve the problem by simply going to bed earlier, but that advice ignores how the teenage body works.

The first reason for a later start is biological. During the teenage years, the bodies internal clock shifts, so most adolescents do not feel sleepy until late at night. A fifteen-year-old who goes to bed at eleven is not necessarily being lazy; he or she is following a natural rhythm. Sleep experts generally advises that teenagers get eight to ten hours of sleep a night. A student who must wake up at six cannot get that much rest.

Tired students are poor learners. When people do not sleep enough, you find it harder to concentrate and to remember new information. Teachers of early classes often describe rows of students who stare at the board but take in very little. A later start would not make lessons easier, but it would give students a better chance of being awake enough to learn.

Critics argue that a later start would cause problems for families. Some things at home might be different, and afternoon sports and clubs would finish later. These concerns are real, but they can be solved. Schools could open their doors at the usual time for students who need to arrive early, and activities could be shortened slightly.

Changing a timetable is never easy, and a later bell would not solve every problem that students face. It would, however, make sure that the first hour of the school day is spent learning rather than fighting sleep. If a school's purpose is to help students learn, it should not begin the day at an hour when many of its students can barely think.

c: waking up in the dark and they arrive
waking up in the dark and arriving
waking up in the dark and arrived
questions.e: Items joined by "and" must be parallel: "waking up ... and arriving." The original mixes an -ing form with "to arrive," "they arrive" adds a new clause that does not fit after "that means," and "arrived" mixes in a past-tense verb.

**Passage VI**
**The Pianist Who Played the Silence**

Karim Nassar never planned to become a jazz musician. He grew up in Alexandria in the 1960s, in an apartment above his father's music shop, and his first teacher allowed him to play nothing but classical exercises. Then, when Karim was fourteen, a sailor traded a box of American records for a used violin from the shop. __[41] One of the records was a recording of__ a jazz pianist playing alone, and Karim listened to it until its grooves were nearly worn smooth.

What fascinated him was the freedom. In classical music, he had been taught to play every note exactly as it was written. On the record, the pianist seemed to invent the music as he went, returning to the melody only after long surprising, detours. Karim began trying to do the same, at first in secret, late at night, with the window open to the sea breeze.

By his twenties, he was playing in hotel lounges along the Corniche. Audiences came for the familiar tunes, but they stayed for his improvisations, that mixed jazz harmonies with the scales of Arabic music. Critics later called the style "Mediterranean blues," a label Karim always disliked. "I am not mixing two things," he once told an interviewer. "I am playing what I hear."

Karim recorded only four albums, and he seldom hardly ever toured. Yet younger musicians who heard him play describe the experience in almost the same words: they remember the silences. He would often stop in the middle of a phrase and let several seconds pass before continuing. Those pauses, he believed, gave listeners time to imagine what might come next.

Today, Karim's piano stands in a small music school in Alexandria, where students are allowed to play it on Friday afternoons. Most of them have never heard his albums. Still, when one of them stops in the middle of a phrase and lets the silence ring, the teachers smile.

questions.e: "Records was a recording" repeats the same idea; "One of the records featured" is concise and clear. "A recorded recording" is even more redundant, and "One record, a record that featured," repeats "record" and leaves the sentence without a main verb.

**The Pianist Who Played the Silence**

Karim Nassar never planned to become a jazz musician. He grew up in Alexandria in the 1960s, in an apartment above his father's music shop, and his first teacher allowed him to play nothing but classical exercises. Then, when Karim was fourteen, a sailor traded a box of American records for a used violin from the shop. One of the records was a recording of a jazz pianist playing alone, and Karim listened to it until its grooves were nearly worn smooth.

What fascinated him was the freedom. In classical music, he had been taught to play every note exactly as it was written. On the record, the pianist seemed to invent the music as he went, returning to the melody only after __[44] long surprising, detours__. Karim began trying to do the same, at first in secret, late at night, with the window open to the sea breeze.

By his twenties, he was playing in hotel lounges along the Corniche. Audiences came for the familiar tunes, but they stayed for his improvisations, that mixed jazz harmonies with the scales of Arabic music. Critics later called the style "Mediterranean blues," a label Karim always disliked. "I am not mixing two things," he once told an interviewer. "I am playing what I hear."

Karim recorded only four albums, and he seldom hardly ever toured. Yet younger musicians who heard him play describe the experience in almost the same words: they remember the silences. He would often stop in the middle of a phrase and let several seconds pass before continuing. Those pauses, he believed, gave listeners time to imagine what might come next.

Today, Karim's piano stands in a small music school in Alexandria, where students are allowed to play it on Friday afternoons. Most of them have never heard his albums. Still, when one of them stops in the middle of a phrase and lets the silence ring, the teachers smile.
questions.q: Question 44 (underlined portion [44]): Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: "Long" and "surprising" both describe "detours" equally (you could say "surprising and long"), so a comma goes between them, but never between the last adjective and its noun. The original puts the comma in the wrong place, "surprising, detours" adds a comma before the noun, and a semicolon cannot separate adjectives.

c: on the same piano his father had bought years earlier

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for **every** question, including the ones you got right: make sure you were right for the right reason, not by luck.
Look at the "By skill" table. Each question is tagged with one of the three ACT English reporting categories: Production of Writing, Knowledge of Language, and Conventions of Standard English.
Write down your weak skills in a notebook (for example: comma splices, add/delete questions, redundancy) and the question numbers where you lost marks.
Conventions of Standard English mistakes: go back to **ACT Punctuation**, **ACT Grammar and Usage** and **Sentence Structure**.
Production of Writing mistakes: go back to **Relevance: Add, Delete and Writer's Goal** and **Organisation: Order and Transitions**.
Knowledge of Language mistakes: go back to **Concision and Redundancy** and **Word Choice and Tone**.
If you ran out of time, reread **How to Attack ACT English** and practise the timing plan, then try ACT English — Practice Test 2 after you have reviewed your weak lessons.
